Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

motivation noun

also motive, motives, incentive, drive (motivation), lack of motivation, what drives someone, highly motivated

classical

Cic. Arch. 23: incitāmentum perīculōrum et labōrum (Lewis & Short)
Tac. Ann. 2.38 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 348

incitāmentum, incitāmentī n.

noun, second declension

incentive, motivation, spur

What urges someone on, with the genitive of what it urges to, or ad: Cicero’s glory is the incitāmentum for facing dangers and toil.

Other words

  • stimulus, stimulī m. — spur, incentive

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Rep. 1.3: ad hanc voluntātem ipsīus nātūrae stimulīs incitāmur (Lewis & Short); Quint. 10.7.16 (Lewis & Short)

    Literally an ox-goad; figuratively what drives one on (also, what torments: see stimulate).

  • studium, studiī n. — eagerness, will (to do something)

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Quint. 1.3.8: studium discendī voluntāte, quae cōgī nōn potest, cōnstat

    The motivation that comes from within: studium discendī, the wish to learn. The same word is “study” and, of judges, “bias” (see bias).

  • causa, causae f. — motive, reason (for doing something)

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Traupman 156 (ratiō)

    A motive in the sense of the reason why someone acts (see reason). Traupman gives ratiō with the genitive, “the reason for”, which classically is the reckoning or principle behind something.

Examples

  • studium discendī voluntāte, quae cōgī nōn potest, cōnstat

    the wish to learn depends on willingness, and willingness cannot be forcedQuint. 1.3.8

See also stimulate, encourage, reason, purpose.

SourcesLewis & Short: incitamentum · Lewis & Short: stimulus · Lewis & Short: studium · Lewis & Short: causa

Quintilian from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-quintilianus); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.
